name: Lena Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a TyreRight centre on the industrial estate, it's one of the national chains, six bays and a little waiting room with a coffee machine that's always broken. Most of my day is tyres, wheel alignments, brake pads, batteries and the yearly safety checks. Head office software tells us which jobs to suggest, so if a car comes in for a puncture, the screen says, offer wipers, offer an alignment. I like the people I work with, I don't like being a salesperson with a torque wrench.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did hairdressing for two years, hated it, and a friend's dad let me help in his garage on Saturdays, and I was hooked. TyreRight took me on as a trainee four years ago, I'm still the most junior fitter who can do more than tyres. I share a flat with my friend Priya, who's a pharmacy assistant, and I've got about four months saved. I use the AI chat thing on my phone now and then, mostly to explain fault codes in plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can stop pretending a chatbot is going to change the world and go back to arguing about real things like wages. At work I'd joke that the upsell screen is the only AI we'll ever get. In the union group chat I'd post something about how the hype was used to keep pay down anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much, which means the same pressures. The chain's been closing branches, two in our region this year, and every month Dean, the branch manager, reads out our upsell numbers like a school report. Even without any clever AI, a computer at head office already decides whether my branch stays open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, stay in the union and keep pushing for the regional pay rise we're due to vote on. I'd keep saving about a hundred and fifty a month. I'd also ask about the alignment and suspension training again, because the fitters who can do that are harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tired, honestly. Relieved there's no big shock, but the normal grind is still a grind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned branch closures. What happens if yours closes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd probably offer me a branch forty minutes away, which means a car I don't have or two buses. There are a few independent garages nearer, but they pay less to start and some of them don't really want a woman in the bay. I'd find something, but it would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your pay didn't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, then eating out with Priya on Fridays. I wouldn't touch the savings unless I had to, because that four months is the only reason I sleep okay.

say: I'd call AI hype that was used to **keep wages down** anyway.
I'd joke that the **upsell screen** is the only AI we'll ever see.
think: The chain is already **closing branches**, and head office software decides which stay.
My **monthly upsell numbers** pressure me more than any new AI.
do: Stay active in the **union** and back the regional pay-rise vote.
Save about **a hundred and fifty** a month and ask again for suspension training.
feel: Feels **tired** and slightly relieved, but the normal grind continues.
S0.quote: Even without any clever AI, a computer at head office already decides whether my branch stays open.
fieldNote: Her pressure comes from **branch closures** and sales targets, not new technology.
She mentions a quiet **sexism** at some independent garages that limits her options.
Her four months of savings are what lets her **sleep**.

steps.text: Vote for the regional pay rise through the union
Save a hundred and fifty from each month's pay
Ask Dean again for wheel alignment and suspension training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the chain will use this to cut staff and call it efficiency. The booking, the quotes, the customer calls and the stock ordering are all thinking tasks, so the two people on the front desk are gone first. I'd be in the union meetings saying we need a deal on this before they bring it in, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it gets me too, a bit later. If the system tells the fitter exactly what to do on every car, they don't need a junior who's still learning, they need someone cheap who follows the screen. The chain won't sack me for being bad with AI, they'll sack me for being the slowest fitter on the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, not just for fault codes, because I'd rather be the fitter who knows the new system. I'd push hard for the suspension and alignment course and maybe get the electric vehicle safety ticket in the first year. Savings up from a hundred and fifty to two hundred a month, and I'd look at the independent garages just to know my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning to scared, if I'm honest. I like my team and I can see some of them not making it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol on the front desk, she's fifty-four and she's the one customers ask for by name. The system would do the booking in seconds, and nobody at head office counts the regulars who come back because of her. I'd fight for her as much as for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the system but also fight it. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I'm not daft, I'll learn it so I'm useful. But I'll also be in the room saying people like Carol need a proper deal, not a leaving card.

say: I'd warn that the chain will **cut staff** and call it efficiency.
I'd tell the union we need **a deal** before the tools arrive.
think: Front-desk jobs go first, and **my job** follows as the system guides every fitter.
I'd be cut for being **slowest on the spreadsheet**, not for lacking skill with AI.
do: Use the **AI tools** properly at work, beyond checking fault codes.
Take the **suspension and alignment** course and the electric vehicle safety ticket.
Raise savings to **two hundred** a month and check independent garages.
feel: Feels **uneasy turning to scared**, especially for colleagues she likes.
S1.quote: The chain won't sack me for being bad with AI, they'll sack me for being the slowest fitter on the spreadsheet.
fieldNote: She plans to **learn and resist** at the same time, and sees no contradiction.
Her concern for **Carol**, an older front-desk worker, is strong and specific.
She expects her own job to be **squeezed** as a slower junior, not instantly replaced.

steps.text: Use the new workshop AI system for every job card
Take the suspension, alignment and electric vehicle safety courses
Push the union for a deal protecting front-desk staff
Raise savings to two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments either step in or lose everyone's trust. I'd post that the profits from AGI should pay for people's living costs while things settle. At work I'd tell everyone to join the union now, today, because in two years it'll be too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 head office won't need Dean, the front desk or half of regional management, and the computer would tell me what to do on every car. By 2031 the robots fit tyres faster than me. I'd have three years left as a pair of hands that a robot is already being trained to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job as long as it lasts and save hard, up to six months if I can, by moving somewhere cheaper with Priya. I'd look for work where a person's face matters, maybe teaching at the college or something in care, because cars won't need me forever. And I'd be at every protest and meeting going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening. Like being on a motorway when the fog comes down fast. I'd be angry too, that nobody planned for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching or care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the one thing I'm good at is explaining things to nervous people. Customers come in scared of a big bill and I talk them through it. Maybe that's the bit that lasts longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine and I've got savings, which would be half true. She'd ask me to move back home and I'd say no, and then probably do it by 2030.

say: I'd say governments must **step in now** or lose everyone's trust.
I'd urge every coworker to **join the union** today.
think: By 2028 head office cuts **managers and front desk**, and software directs my work.
I'd have about **three years** before robots fit tyres faster than me.
do: Move somewhere **cheaper** with Priya to reach six months of savings.
Look into **teaching or care**, where explaining to nervous people matters.
feel: Feels **frightened**, like driving into sudden fog, and angry at the lack of planning.
S2.quote: I'd have three years left as a pair of hands that a robot is already being trained to replace.
fieldNote: She sees her **explaining skill** as the part of her that lasts longest.
She admits she'd likely **move home** by 2030 despite saying no.
Her anger is aimed at **governments** that failed to prepare, more than at the chain.

steps.text: Move to a cheaper flat with Priya
Push savings towards six months of costs
Ask the college about teaching motor vehicle basics
Join protests calling for AGI profits to fund living costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and no excuse, so let's write the rules now. Retraining money, a slower roll-out in workplaces, and a say for workers. I'd be pushing that line in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three for robots gives me about eight years in the bays. That's long enough to get from junior to decent, but maybe not long enough to matter. Eight years is enough time to stop being the junior, and maybe not enough time for that to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the alignment and electric courses in the first year, so I'm not the obvious one to cut. I'd ask the college about part-time teacher training for motor vehicle classes in year two or three. Savings up to five months, and I'd stay in the flat with Priya for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but organised. It's like having a deadline at work, I hate it but I know what to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd make it my homework partner for the courses. I'd see it as getting ready for a world where it's everywhere. I'd still check it, though, because it's been wrong on my fault codes before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want the union to win in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retraining paid for by the companies that save money, and notice before any job changes. Also something for the older ones, like Carol, so they don't fall off a cliff.

say: I'd say **five years** leaves no excuse not to write the rules.
I'd push the union for **retraining money** and a worker say in roll-outs.
think: I'd get about **eight years** in the bays before robots arrive.
That's enough to **stop being junior**, but maybe not enough to matter.
do: Finish the **alignment and electric** courses in the first year.
Start **part-time teacher training** for motor vehicle classes in year two.
Build savings to **five months** while staying in the shared flat.
feel: Feels **nervous but organised**, like facing a deadline at work.
S3.quote: Eight years is enough time to stop being the junior, and maybe not enough time for that to matter.
fieldNote: The extra time makes her **plan a second career** in teaching early.
She'd use **AI** as a **study partner** but still double-checks it.
Her concern for **older colleagues** stays central to her politics.

steps.text: Finish the alignment and electric vehicle courses this year
Use the AI chat tool as a study partner for courses
Ask the union to win retraining paid for by companies
Grow savings to five months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly and fairly, if we start now. I'd put it to the union that we need a ten-year plan, not a press release. Online I'd share stuff about countries that are planning well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm thirty-seven when AGI arrives and forty when the robots come. That's a whole career stage I could build in something else. With ten years warning, I'd stop thinking of myself as a mechanic and start thinking of myself as someone who teaches mechanics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the courses, get good, then move into teaching at the college within five years. I'd keep a weekend shift at a garage so my skills stay fresh. I'd save steadily and maybe think about a small flat of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, more hopeful. There's still sadness in it, because I love being in the bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach once robots can fix cars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe how to work with them, or how to look after them. Someone has to teach the next lot, even if the job changes shape. And there'll be old cars around for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a sixteen-year-old thinking of becoming a mechanic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do it, but learn the electrics and learn the computers. And join a union on day one.

say: I'd ask the union for a **ten-year plan**, not a press release.
I'd share examples of countries **planning well** for the change.
think: I'd be **forty** when robots arrive, with time to build another career.
I'd start seeing myself as someone who **teaches mechanics**.
do: Move into **teaching** at the college within five years.
Keep a **weekend garage shift** so hands-on skills stay fresh.
Save steadily towards a **small flat** of her own.
feel: Feels **calmer and more hopeful**, with some sadness about leaving the bay.
S4.quote: With ten years warning, I'd stop thinking of myself as a mechanic and start thinking of myself as someone who teaches mechanics.
fieldNote: With a decade, she expects a **safe landing** in teaching, so her mood eases.
She still loves the **hands-on work** and plans to keep a foot in it.
Her advice to young people is **electrics, computers** and union membership.

steps.text: Move into teaching at the local college within five years
Keep a weekend shift at a garage
Save steadily towards a small flat of her own

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years is no time for anyone, least of all the chain, which would just cut and cut. What would help is retraining that's actually paid for, a safety net that covers rent, and a union that's strong before it happens, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women in the trade. It took me years to get in the bay. I fought for four years to be taken seriously in a garage, and I'm not ready for a robot to undo that in two.

headlineQuote: I fought for four years to be taken seriously in a garage, and I'm not ready for a robot to undo that in two.
portrait: Lena is a **junior fitter** at a national tyre-and-brakes chain, after leaving hairdressing.
She shares a flat with Priya and has about **four months** saved.
She is a committed **union member** who uses AI now and then for fault codes.
She expects to be **squeezed out** as a slower junior and worries deeply for older colleagues.
With more warning she plans a move into **teaching** motor vehicle skills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the chain would cut fast and there'd be no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining**, a safety net that covers rent, and a strong **union** in place beforehand.
